title: Knowledge Check 11: Lessons 81-90
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 81-90 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A program's benefits accumulate over a three-year horizon, and the question is how to compare cash saved at different points in time. Which return measure is built for that?
options: Return on investment, which divides net benefit by total cost
Payback period, which counts months until the cash returns
Net present value, which discounts future cash to today
Total cost of ownership, which sums the fully loaded cost side
questions.explanation: Return on investment hides timing, and payback ignores cash beyond the break-even point. Net present value discounts every future dollar to today, which is what makes it the measure for a multi-year horizon.

questions.question: Why does cost per accepted output make a stronger denominator than cost per token or cost per seat?
options: It measures only the model spend, so it isolates the cost that scales with volume
It divides total cost by the work that a human accepts without redoing
It removes the need to estimate rework, since failures are not counted as outputs
It tracks how cheaply the model generates text, which is the figure finance reviews
questions.explanation: Cost per token is the bill and cost per seat is a software habit; neither says whether the spend was worthwhile. Dividing total cost by accepted outputs, including the rework failures require, is what makes the unit economics computable.

questions.question: An agent workflow stays net positive across a wide range of auto-clear rates. What carries that result?
options: A low enough token price that the inference line stops mattering
A high reversal cost that protects the workflow from being undone
A larger build budget that spreads platform cost over many runs
Packet preparation that shortens each remaining human decision
questions.explanation: The value comes less from autonomy than from packet preparation that makes every remaining human decision faster. The agent does not have to be right to be useful; it has to shorten the next decision.

questions.question: Which set of measures best describes adoption of a new agent workflow?
options: Speed of adoption, ultimate utilization, and proficiency
Login count, session length, and daily page views
Training completion, attendance, and a satisfaction score
Number of champions, budget spent, and tickets closed
questions.explanation: A login count confirms a browser session, not that the new path was used. Adoption is described by speed of adoption, ultimate utilization and proficiency, and those three move independently.

questions.question: A team reports that every analyst finished the required training session and asks to go live. What does a working readiness gate require in addition?
options: A completion dashboard with per-person timestamps so the sponsor can see training landed
A scored dry run on real cases with a stated threshold and a dated retry
A second refresher session scheduled thirty days after launch to review the material
A signed attendance sheet recording which analysts were present at every session
questions.explanation: Finishing a session shows that information was received, not that it can be applied under real conditions. A working gate uses real cases, scores the decisions against a stated threshold, and gives anyone who fails a dated retry.

questions.question: A weekly review has produced meeting notes for two months with no eval cases, policy changes or tool fixes. What is the correct reading and fix?
options: The agent is performing well, so the meetings should continue as passive monitoring
The intake form needs more free-text fields so analysts can describe problems in detail
The loop is capturing without closing, so a corrected answer must become an eval case
The review should move to a monthly cadence so each item has time to mature
questions.explanation: The output of a feedback loop is a change to the system, so a loop that produces only notes is decorative. Promoting a corrected answer into the offline eval set turns a complaint into a regression test.

questions.question: An engineer presents a live demo of an agent succeeding on several cases and offers it as proof the design is sound. Why does a reviewer discount that?
options: Because demos are not allowed in a design review, since only the packet may be presented
Because a demo proves a path exists once, not that it is the normal path
Because the sample was too small to compute a rate, so the whole run must be repeated
Because the output cannot be reproduced, which makes the demo inadmissible as evidence
questions.explanation: A demo shows that a path exists on one day; under stochastic behavior it does not show that the path is the normal path. The evidence page therefore carries a pass rate, a sample size and one honest failing case.

questions.question: A reviewer challenges a decision that sits behind a clean boundary and is cheap to undo. How should the author handle it?
options: Defend it firmly, because conceding anything early signals the design is weak
Park it for a separate meeting so the current review can still reach its decision
Concede it early and visibly, and spend attention on the costly decisions
Escalate it to the decision owner, since any disagreement needs a formal path
questions.explanation: The reversal-cost column decides which arguments are worth having. Cheap-to-undo decisions are conceded early and visibly, which buys credibility for the expensive, hard-to-reverse decisions.

questions.question: A review closes with conditional approval, but one condition names no owner and no date. How should the team read that?
options: As a normal approval, since owners can be assigned later during delivery planning
As a deferral of the whole design until the evidence page is complete
As a request to replace the low-confidence record before the pilot starts
As a rejection in disguise, since it cannot be enforced and will be missed
questions.explanation: Approval with conditions is the normal outcome, but every condition needs an owner and a date. A condition that cannot be enforced is a rejection in disguise.

questions.question: When scoring candidate workflows, which two criteria act as hard reject gates that no total score can rescue?
options: High volume and high variance
A named owner and a measurable baseline
Low error asymmetry and high volume
High variance and low error asymmetry together
questions.explanation: A measurable baseline with labelled history is what lets you score the agent, and a named owner is what gets it shipped; no total score rescues either one. The other screens shape the design but do not reject a candidate outright.

questions.question: Autonomy is set per action rather than per agent. What does that mean for one agent with several tools?
options: The agent holds a single autonomy level, decided at design time and applied to every tool
The autonomy level rises automatically as the agent's measured accuracy improves
Each action gets its own rung, evidence to climb and a blast-radius cap
Autonomy is set per workflow, since actions inside one agent cannot differ
questions.explanation: Autonomy belongs to actions, not to an agent. One agent can sit at different rungs across its tools, each with its own permitting evidence, a blast-radius cap, and a descent scheduled in advance.

questions.question: Why does the evaluation plan have to exist before the architecture is settled?
options: Because reviewers require a signed metric list before they will read the architecture page
Because the model judge cannot be configured until every metric has a numeric threshold
Because thresholds must be written qualitatively so reviewers can apply their own judgment
Because the eval set shapes the architecture, so measuring later is a costly retrofit
questions.explanation: The eval set shapes the architecture, so building first and measuring later is an expensive retrofit. A held-out split, adversarial cases, and metrics written as numbers with consequences have to be decided up front.

questions.question: An engineer proposes a single tool that accepts a free-form query string and can reach any data the team might need. Why is that rejected?
options: Because a single tool increases the token cost of the tool definitions on every turn
Because a free-form query tool is unbounded access rather than a scoped capability
Because one protocol server must host one tool, so a broad tool cannot span systems
Because free-form arguments cannot be validated, which makes latency unpredictable
questions.explanation: One tool per action, never one tool per system. A broad query tool is unbounded access with a friendly name, so the tool layer exposes named tools that take validated identifiers and return a fixed shape.

questions.question: A network timeout is retried on a write and one customer receives two return labels for a single case. Which rule prevents this?
options: A per-tool timeout with retries and jitter applied to read tools only
An iteration cap that bounds how many times a write may be attempted
An idempotency key so a retried write returns the original result
A shadow mode that records the draft next to what the analyst actually sent
questions.explanation: Every write takes an idempotency key, and no write retries without one. The key lets the server recognize a retry and return the stored result instead of performing the action twice.

questions.question: A single path is producing wrong results while the rest of the traffic is fine. Which control matches the blast radius?
options: The global flag, because any quality problem justifies falling back to the old queue for all traffic
The tool flag on a read tool, since the problem likely originates in the underlying data
The feature flag, because lowering the rollout percentage removes the affected drafts
A workflow flag that stops the one affected path while other traffic continues
questions.explanation: Kill switches are separated by blast radius: a tool flag for one tool, a workflow flag for one path while other traffic continues, and a global flag for all traffic. A feature flag controls who sees a path, not whether the path exists.

questions.question: Customer complaints and satisfaction are flat, but the rate at which humans edit the agent's drafts has doubled over three weeks. What does that signal?
options: Nothing actionable, because quality should be judged by customer satisfaction rather than edit metrics
A quality regression not yet visible to customers, since edit rate moves before complaints do
A threshold set too low, so the fix is to raise the edit-rate target to match the regional baseline
Retrieval drift that can only be fixed by rebuilding the search index from scratch
questions.explanation: Edit rate is the early-warning metric because it moves within days of a retrieval or prompt regression, well before complaint rates move. A rising edit rate with flat complaints is a system that got worse and nobody outside the team has noticed yet.

questions.question: A severity 3 quality incident is closed with several prompt edits and no new test coverage. What is wrong with that closure?
options: The incident should have been escalated a severity, since any post-launch quality drop is customer facing
Prompt edits kept in a console rather than version control make the closure unauditable
Nothing, because a prompt edit is faster to apply than a code change and the item has an owner
Every postmortem should add at least one eval case and at most one prompt change
questions.explanation: The ratio keeps incidents from becoming an unreadable pile of prompt edits with no test coverage. At least one eval case converts the incident into a regression test, and at most one prompt change keeps the instruction set comprehensible.

questions.question: The error budget burns most of its monthly allowance in two days after a bad change. What is the correct response?
options: Stop shipping changes until the budget recovers, rather than ship faster to fix things
Spend the remaining budget on the fix, since a budget exists to fund corrective changes
Roll the rollout back a stage and then resume shipping at the same rate
Raise the objective so the burn no longer breaches the documented threshold
questions.explanation: An objective is a budget to spend, and when it burns down the response is to stop shipping changes rather than to ship faster. Raising an objective to escape a burn defeats the purpose of having one.

questions.question: What distinguishes an agentic workflow from an autonomous pipeline?
options: The workflow can act without approval, while the pipeline always requires a person to start each run
The workflow fixes the sequence, while the pipeline moves work unattended and survives a crash
The workflow runs on a schedule, while the pipeline is triggered by a person each time
The workflow tolerates crashes, while the pipeline is expected to restart from the beginning
questions.explanation: An agentic workflow runs model and tool calls through a fixed code path, so the sequence is set at design time. An autonomous pipeline moves work between systems unattended, and its own failure is lost or duplicated work rather than a wrong answer.

questions.question: A retry is added to a step that appends a row, and a slow period produces two rows for one case. Which rule did the retry violate?
options: Retries belong on the whole run rather than on an individual tool call
A retry must be bounded by the error budget before it is allowed to run
A retry is safe only when applying it twice equals applying it once
Fresh data is always preferable, so the step should have waited for input
questions.explanation: An idempotent mutation is what makes a retry safe: applying the change twice must equal applying it once. A retry on a plain append produces a duplicate row, so a timeout turns into a data quality incident.

questions.question: A loop proposes to automatically roll back a prompt change after a quality regression. Why should that be a person's decision?
options: Because rollbacks are safe once they are dry-run against recent traffic
Because a rollback should always be paired with a notification to the quality owner
Because the correct repair is to rewrite the affected records rather than the prompt
Because it changes how processed cases should be read, which belongs to a person
questions.explanation: Rolling back a prompt change rewrites the behavior behind cases already processed, which is a data-reinterpretation decision. Anything that changes how already-written data should be interpreted belongs to a person.

questions.question: Why do shared standards cut integration cost?
options: Because custom links grow with pairs of systems, while a shared standard needs one implementation each
Because a standard removes the commercial questions of liability, data use and uptime from the relationship
Because a published protocol makes two compliant implementations agree on what a message means
Because a standard lets any system connect without authentication once both sides share the protocol
questions.explanation: Adapters are counted per pair, so cost grows with pairs of systems rather than with systems. One shared standard needs a single implementation per system and cuts the pairwise count sharply.

questions.question: In a delegated, human-not-present purchase, what does a signed intent mandate accomplish?
options: It replaces the cart mandate with a single reusable authorization code
It records the user's instruction only after the purchase has already settled
It is verifiable pre-authorized proof that lets the agent act within limits
It requires the user to approve each purchase in real time before payment settles
questions.explanation: A delegated intent mandate carries the conditions, such as price limits and timing, and serves as verifiable pre-authorized proof. That lets the agent generate a cart mandate on the user's behalf once those conditions are met, which is what separates a delegation from a blank check.

questions.question: A verdict arrives from a counterparty's agent whose internals you cannot inspect, and it would trigger an automatic refund. What is the right control?
options: Trust the verdict, because the counterparty's published card declared the relevant skill
Show the verdict to a person, because an opaque result can never be validated
Request every skill the card advertises so the verdict can be re-derived independently
Treat the artifact as untrusted input, with provenance, a threshold and a rule
questions.explanation: An artifact from an opaque counterparty is untrusted input, the same way a web form is. Provenance, a threshold and a named rule for what may be automated keep a verdict from firing an irreversible refund.

questions.question: A ninety-day plan is organized as three 30-day arcs. What makes an arc a real unit of plan rather than a list of things to try?
options: It ends with a demonstration that impresses a reviewing room
It closes on one artifact and one number that can fail
It groups the tools you plan to try by how new they are
It names the frameworks you intend to evaluate carefully
questions.explanation: A roadmap is a dated sequence of artifacts, each with a number attached, so an arc is only real when it closes on something measurable that can fail. A list of tools or frameworks produces an opinion rather than a number.

questions.question: A rule must never be violated, no matter what the model decides on a given run. Where should that rule be enforced?
options: In the system prompt, restated at the start of every session
In the evaluation set, as a case that scores the behavior afterward
In hooks, deny rules and tests that run regardless of the model
In the design packet, so a later reviewer can confirm it existed
questions.explanation: An instruction the model reads is non-deterministic and can be declined on a given run, so it cannot carry a rule that must always hold. Rules with no exceptions belong in the harness, which executes hooks, deny rules and tests whether or not the model cooperates.

questions.question: A builder wants to know whether the workflow she built can keep producing numbers after she moves to another team. What test settles it?
options: The held-out split scores above the threshold written in the packet
The decision records list what was rejected as well as what was chosen
The evaluation suite runs on its own schedule whether or not anyone is watching
Somebody else runs the workflow for a week, with you reachable but not present
questions.explanation: The handoff test is whether a second person can operate the system while the builder is reachable but not present, which shows the work outlives its author. A plan with no handoff step was a personal project with a deadline.

questions.question: An architect must tell the difference between a capability limit and a control. Which item is a control?
options: A prompt line that tells the agent never to send email to a customer
A deny rule that blocks the send tool entirely
A named on-call owner recorded in the runbook
A quarterly re-label of the held-out evaluation set
questions.explanation: A capability limit is an instruction the model reads and can decline on a given run, while a control holds regardless of what the model decides. A deny rule that blocks the send tool is enforced outside the model, so it is a control.

questions.question: An action is capped at draft-only so a human must approve every send, but unapproved sends keep occurring. Where is the real permission set?
options: In the autonomy rung recorded in the design document
In the evaluation set that scores the action after the fact
In the credential scope that the tool actually runs under
In the governance policy approved by the review board
questions.explanation: A bounded autonomy rung does not bound an action if the credential behind it can write. The scope of the service account is the real permission, and it is usually set somewhere the design document never mentions.

questions.question: An architect is choosing the two areas to go deep on. What rule applies when she is accountable for a system already in production?
options: One of the two areas must come from the control shelf.
Both areas must come from the shelf with the nearest failure.
The two areas must be the newest protocol and the newest tool.
Both areas must come from the build shelf.
questions.explanation: Deep areas are picked by exposure and visibility, then constrained by accountability: one of the two must come from the control shelf, because that is where generalist knowledge becomes expensive. A deep area without an artifact within thirty days is only a reading list.
